rationale: Directly explains the ordered feature-downsell path after rejection, including re-upselling, further feature removal, a desire check, and a payment-plan fallback.
Directly identifies less quantity as a feature downsell and explains how reducing scope and price can preserve the sale.
Directly provides membership-bonus options, including status, anchored bonuses, and stacked bonus value.
Directly explains using a waived onboarding fee and term commitment to carry customers past an early churn point.
Directly defines rolling a prior purchase into the next offer; the useful passage crosses the framework chunk boundary below the automatic overlap threshold.
Directly explains how continuity, standalone bonuses, and bulk prepayment can create enough up-front cash to offset acquisition costs and shorten payback.
Directly explains how a membership bonus can secure a three-, six-, or twelve-month commitment and increase committed revenue relative to a standalone sale.
Directly defines the next-offer pattern after an earlier purchase and the three decisions required to apply it.
Directly says an upsell is the next offer and that a classic upsell is presented when the customer becomes aware of the next problem.
Directly explains which fulfillment costs reduce gross profit and therefore constrains whether a high-fulfillment buy-X-get-Y offer is affordable.
Directly explains how up-front bonus pricing, recurring revenue, and bulk prepayment fit together to offset acquisition costs in a money-model stack.
Directly describes a conditional pay-later offer that lets a skeptical customer experience and verify a result before being charged.
Directly explains that attraction offers use free or discounted value to turn unfamiliar prospects into customers, which fits the stated trust barrier.
Directly explains that higher-priced offers require a longer runway of free value before a prospect is ready to buy.
Directly explains how presenting a credible premium offer first makes a similar, lower-priced core offer easier to evaluate and buy.
Directly explains that increasing customer value is what allows a business to afford more acquisition spend.
Discusses cash timing and bonus-versus-continuity pricing, but does not identify what kind of bonus would make the membership more valuable.
